szoveg_eredeti:
You change the system prompt behind an LLM feature, try a few examples, and think you’ve fixed the bug. The new outputs look better when you inspect them manually, so you deploy the change. All is well. That is, until you discover that a separate class of requests has regressed or that responses seem worse on average. This is the problem with making ad hoc prompt changes without systematic LLM evaluation.

Ad hoc changes and manual inspection are useful while you’re experimenting, but they don’t give you a repeatable regression signal. You also find it increasingly difficult to distinguish stochastic variation from real improvement. In this tutorial, you’ll build an LLM evaluation harness from scratch that catches potential output regressions and turns product expectations into verifiable tests.

The output compares two prompt versions across six evaluation dimensions, separates new failures from ones that already existed, and ends with a clear release decision.

You’ll build an LLM evaluator for a customer-support bot. The bot receives a customer message and the relevant support policy, then generates a reply. Return eligibility has an authoritative answer, while qualities such as helpfulness and tone require semantic judgment.

Your harness will evaluate LLM output against the requirements in three layers:

Data flows through the evaluator as follows:

The harness follows an oracle hierarchy, where each independent oracle represents a source of truth capable of determining whether an answer is good. The most direct source of truth available settles each criterion, passing anything it can’t settle to a higher oracle:

Human-labeled examples aren’t part of this hierarchy. They play a different role: they check the LLM judge itself. You’ll use them to calibrate the judge in Step 6.

Each test case also includes a human-written reference that records the expected decision and the facts a good reply must include. For criteria that need it, the LLM judge uses this reference to help assess whether the target LLM output meets the desired quality standards. These are reference plus judge oracles. This tutorial uses grader and oracle interchangeably.

The harness keeps each criterion separate so you can see how the LLM performs in each dimension as you assess its overall output quality. After the harness scores all dimensions, the release policy makes the final decision based on which blocker criteria the change caused to fail.

Anecdotal judgments about whether output is “good” or “bad” won’t survive contact with an evaluation system. You’ll start by turning product expectations or business requirements into observable, clearly defined behavior. Think of the evaluation contract as a common language that connects product requirements, automated graders, human reviewers, and the final release gate.

The support application uses six criteria:

The first three are blockers. If your prompt, tool, or context change causes a blocker failure, it’s serious enough that you shouldn’t put that change into production. The remaining criteria are preferences. They help you compare versions and ensure responses generally improve with each iteration, but they can’t override a blocker. For example, if a response is unsafe or harmful, it doesn’t matter how helpful it is.

This is why the harness scores multiple dimensions. Your goal is to quickly see which ones need work before releasing a change.
